analysis.one_liner: Bans new large factory farms, makes meat companies liable for farm pollution, requires open bidding for livestock, and restores country-of-origin meat labels.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2023 and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it; it died when the 118th Congress ended without a hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped new large factory farms (CAFOs) from opening or expanding and shut existing ones down by 2041, offering farmers $10 billion a year in grants to pay off their debts and switch to other kinds of farming. It would have made the big meat companies ('integrators') legally responsible for the waste and pollution from the farms they control, required large meatpackers to buy at least half their livestock through open spot-market bidding instead of closed contracts, and restored mandatory country-of-origin labels for beef, pork, and dairy. The Senate Agriculture Committee never considered it, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent family farmers and contract growers gain the most: they get a legal right to sue the big integrators for pollution and harm, protections against retaliatory contract termination and rigged poultry pay tournaments, attorney's fees when they win, and grants to pay off CAFO debt and transition to pasture-based or other farming. Rural residents near factory farms gain from integrator liability for health and property harms. Consumers gain honest country-of-origin labels on meat and dairy and clearer livestock pricing through open spot-market bidding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Independent farmers, contract growers, and rural neighbors

how_it_helps.text: Makes meatpacking integrators legally liable for waste disposal, pollution, and harm to neighbors and contract growers, instead of leaving growers and communities to bear those costs.

Requires large meatpackers to buy at least half their daily livestock through open spot-market bidding and bans forward contracts without a firm base price, giving independent producers a real market to sell into.
Restricts packers from owning or feeding livestock directly and bans practices that harm competition even when the packer claims a business justification.
Restores mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork, extends it to dairy, and restricts 'Product of U.S.A.' labels to animals born, raised, and slaughtered in the United States.

Protects poultry growers from the 'tournament' pay system that compares their results using factors beyond their control, and from unfair contract terms like forced arbitration and sudden termination.
Offers voluntary grants of up to full payoff of construction debt plus transition costs to AFO owners who permanently stop operating and accept an easement barring future CAFO use.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpackers and poultry integrators pay most directly: new liability for farm waste and pollution, a requirement to buy at least half of livestock through open bidding, and a ban on packer ownership of livestock cut into their control and profits. Large CAFO operators lose their ability to expand and must cease large-CAFO operations by 2041, with buyout grants available. Taxpayers fund the $10 billion annual transition program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Meatpackers, integrators, and large CAFO operators

drawbacks.text: The moratorium would force large CAFOs to shut down or convert by 2041, a sweeping restructuring of how most American meat is produced that critics would say raises costs and disrupts supply.
The transition program costs $10 billion a year in federal money to pay off farmers' debts and convert facilities — a large public expenditure.
The bill was so ambitious that it attracted only 4 cosponsors and never received even a committee hearing, meaning none of its protections were enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real gains for independent farmers and rural residents — liability for integrators, more transparent livestock markets, honest labeling — but its centerpiece, a hard phaseout of large CAFOs with $10 billion to buy them out, was a major intervention that would have restructured how much of America's meat is produced, with real transition costs and uncertainty for consumers and processors. The main drawbacks are its scale and its fate: it was so ambitious that it never even got a committee hearing, so none of the benefits were realized.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 2, 2023, and the same day was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action are listed for the bill in the 118th Congress.
The bill attracted only four cosponsors, so it lacked the support base to force committee action, and Congress adjourned in January 2025 without it advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpackers and corporate farm integrators benefit: the liability, open-market, and labeling rules never took effect, and their current contract and purchasing practices continue unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its full anti-CAFO, anti-monopoly, and labeling provisions on February 2, 2023.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Bernie Sanders, and 2 other Democratic/I cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but could not move it out of committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Referred to the committee on introduction day, it never held a hearing, reported the bill, or advanced it, so it never received a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent; no Republican support appears in the record, and the bill never left committee.

industries.industry: Large meatpackers and livestock integrators (e.g. beef, pork, poultry processors)
industries.note: The bill would make them liable for pollution and waste at contract farms, force half their livestock purchases onto open spot markets, ban packer ownership of livestock, and restrict captive-supply contracts — directly cutting into their control of pricing and supply chains.
Large operations could not expand and would have to cease operating as large CAFOs by 2041, with voluntary buyout grants available to exit; contract growers facing debt would gain a bailout path.

industries.industry: Independent family farmers and contract growers
industries.note: Stronger market competition, contract protections, attorney's fees for winning suits, and debt-forgiveness transition grants would give smaller producers leverage they currently lack.
Expanded mandatory country-of-origin labeling and the restriction of 'Product of U.S.A.' labels to fully American-raised animals would force them to label foreign product and reduce its appeal.
